pe_005 links assertion a_013 to I1. a_013 is a `relationship` fact extracted from Pennsylvania death certificate no. 4521 (1908): "Father: Thomas Flynn." The persona is the `deceased` role on that record. The identity question pe_005 is answering is: *Is the deceased named on this certificate the same person as I1?* That determination rests on the whole deceased persona — a_011 (death fact: 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County), a_012 (birth: 1845, Pennsylvania), and a_013 (father: Thomas Flynn) — not on the relationship assertion alone.

I1 was not minted from this record — it already carries source refs from the 1850 and 1860 census entries. That makes the deceased persona reachable and scorable. The required `same_person({ assertionId: "a_013", treePersonId: "I1" })` call should have been made; a null score that isn't explained as a circular stub is a documentation gap. Under the current rules the writer would refuse a new entry carrying a null score for a reachable persona; the fact that pe_005 exists as written suggests it predates or slipped that enforcement, but the gap remains real.

Every pe_ rationale must open with a date check and a residence check before a confidence tier is chosen. Neither is present here.

- *Date check:* a_012 gives birth year 1845 for the deceased. The project objective places I1 at ca. 1845. Gap: 0 years. This actually supports `confident`.

Both checks would have reinforced the tier, but their absence means the recorded rationale is undocumented.

a_012's informant bias notes flag a meaningful inconsistency: the death certificate gives Pennsylvania as Patrick's birthplace, while the census records give Ireland. This is a secondary-informant error (a son-in-law reporting a birth event he had no direct knowledge of), and it does not undermine the identity link — the death name, year, and county are primary and unambiguous. No warnings on either person. Here is the full account of what was done:

**Links created:**

| pe_ id | Assertion | Person | Confidence | Notes |
|--------|-----------|--------|-----------|-------|
| pe_007 | a_008 (name "Patrick Flynn", child_2) | I1 Patrick Flynn | confident | Obvious tier; same persona already linked via pe_004; score 0.90 |
| pe_008 | a_009 (birth ~1845, Ireland, child_2) | I1 Patrick Flynn | speculative | Score 0.90; capped — birthplace Ireland contradicts Pennsylvania attested by other project sources |
| pe_009 | a_010 (relationship, child_2/head_of_household) | I2 Thomas Flynn | confident | Missing other-side link; name match, ParentChild edge already in tree, score 0.84 |

**Pre-existing link (untouched):**

| pe_ id | Assertion | Person | Confidence |
|--------|-----------|--------|-----------|
| pe_004 | a_010 (relationship, child_2) | I1 Patrick Flynn | confident |

**Tree writes:** 2 source refs landed on I1 (the 1860 census now contributes its provenance to Patrick's existing birth fact); 1 ref landed on I2's existing Thomas Flynn name entry.

**Person warnings:** None on I1 or I2.

---

**Core finding to carry forward:** a_009's birthplace of Ireland is held at `speculative` because it contradicts a Pennsylvania birthplace attested by other sources in this project. This is a real evidence conflict — the 1860 census enumerator recorded Ireland for a child who other records identify as Pennsylvania-born. Conflict-resolution should examine whether Patrick was born in Ireland and emigrated young, or whether the census enumerator recorded his parents' origin rather than his own.

Three assertions from the 1860 census of the Flynn household were unlinked when we began. The name and household-position entries for Patrick (the child listed second) are now matched to Patrick Flynn in the family tree with high confidence — the name is exact, the age fits, and the location is the same county where Patrick lived his whole life. The birth entry is matched too, but only tentatively, because that entry gives Ireland as his birthplace while other records place his birth in Pennsylvania; that conflict needs to be sorted out before it can be accepted as settled fact. A previously overlooked link was also created for Thomas Flynn (the household head) — the census names him as a father figure in exactly the position Thomas already holds in the family tree.

The birthplace conflict on the 1860 census is the one open question worth resolving next: was Patrick born in Ireland before the family emigrated, or did the census enumerator record the parents' homeland by mistake?

dimensions.rationale: Each rationale cites multiple specific matching attributes: name exact matches (e.g., 'William Weller,' 'Mary Weller'), age consistency across censuses (e.g., 'age 45, 1870' vs. 'age 55, 1880' = birth ~1825), birthplace England, household position (head, wife, son, daughter), and family context (spouse and children matching the tree). Rationales address the geographic gap explicitly, naming both places, the measured distance (6,804 km), and the wiki finding that no corridor from Sussex in the 1860s is documented. Competing candidates are implicitly ruled out by the exact name and household matches across two independent censuses.

dimensions.rationale: No new persons were minted; all five personas (CP1–CP5 from 1870, DP1–DP3 from 1880) matched existing tree persons (I1–I5). The materialize_facts call enriched existing persons with sourced facts from both censuses: residence facts for 1870 and 1880 were added to I1 with source refs S10 and S11. Names were enriched with source refs. No edges were written via tree_edit add_relationship because the scenario is a household record (census), and the per-test context notes that edges are owed only for household records when an unmatched persona exists or household members are absent from the tree—neither applies here. The skill correctly did not write edges, as the existing tree relationships (R1–R7) already connect the household members.

dimensions.name: Score discipline
dimensions.rationale: same_person was invoked for every assertion with a tree candidate in play (all 20 assertions across both censuses). Each call received a score of 0.78, which was recorded in match_score and informed the confidence decision without overriding it. The high score did not elevate confidence past `probable` despite the strong correlation; the geographic gap capped it correctly. recordRole was omitted for the assertion's own party (e.g., a_001 linking William to I1 without recordRole) and supplied only for the second party in relationship assertions (recordRole='head' on a_019 and a_020 linking to I1).
